description: Finding Earth's frontiers. Paving the way beyond.
summary:
An Earth analog is a place at the right time. NASA plans its Moon base near the lunar South Pole, where the Sun never climbs more than a few degrees above the horizon: at Mons Mouton it stays between 0° and 6.9°. Long shadows and hard contrast are what navigation cameras, rovers and astronauts must work in, and they are the hardest conditions to reproduce on Earth. At NASA's Arizona test site the Sun crosses that band for at most 43 minutes at a stretch, so South Pole moonwalks are rehearsed at night under spotlights.

The Seasonal Analog Planner finds where and when on Earth the real Sun sits that low for hours each day. Using ten years of NASA weather data, it ranks 14 Earth sites by the usable test days a 14-day campaign can expect, and shows each site on a 3D globe beside the Moon. A fidelity card for every site states where the analogy holds, where it breaks down and what is impossible on Earth. It gives field-test leads a measured answer to where and when to test.
details:
Live site: https://nasa-space-apps-2026-liart.vercel.app/

WHAT IT DOES

The planner answers one question for the person who leads a field test of a lunar South Pole surface system: where and when on Earth should we test this, how faithful will it be, and how many usable days will we get?

- Planner: choose a lunar target (Mons Mouton or Malapert Massif), a cloud limit, a wind-chill limit and a month. The 14 Earth sites are ranked by the usable test days a 14-day campaign can expect. A 3D globe shows the low-sun ring at any hour, and a Compare view shows the same moment on Earth and on the Moon.

- Site pages: the best 14-day window, the daily sun path, a 12-month calendar and campaign odds. Each page prints as a one-page card and exports as CSV.

- Fidelity card: rates each condition as match, partial, breaks down or impossible on Earth, with its data source.

- Methods: the validation checks, the rules, the data and the limits.

HOW IT WORKS

- Sun band: from 0° to the highest the Sun climbs at the lunar target (6.9° at Mons Mouton, 5.5° at Malapert Massif). Sun positions on Earth are calculated every 5 minutes and checked against NREL SPA to within 0.02°.

- Usable day: the Sun stays in the band for at least 2 unbroken hours, with cloud, wind, wind chill and precipitation within limits during that time.

- Campaign odds: ten years of hourly data (2016 to 2025). The best window is scored on years held out from its choice.

- Terrain: slope from LRO LOLA at the lunar target compared with the Copernicus DEM at the Earth site.

RESULTS

At the default settings the best windows are in the High Arctic in spring and autumn: Peary Land, Greenland (4.5 usable days of 14), Kronprins Christian Land (3.8), Vestfold Hills, Antarctica (3.7), Inland Ellesmere Island (3.3) and Devon Island (3.0). NASA's Arizona site gets 0: the terrain matches, the light never does. Four of these five sites have no published use as a Moon or Mars analog that we could find.

LIMITS, STATED

In the Arctic, the weeks with long low sun also have snow on the ground, so the light matches the Moon while the surface does not. The Sun's speed across the sky and the black sky break down on Earth; gravity, vacuum and radiation are impossible. This version covers one test objective and two lunar targets; Mars targets are a next step.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Analog sites are usually treated as fixed places. We treat an analog as a place and a season, and we count the days a team can use.

TOOLS

Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray, rasterio) for the data pipeline; Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and three.js for the website; pytest and GitHub Actions for tests; Vercel for hosting. The pipeline calculates everything in advance and writes static files, so the site needs no server.

USE OF AI

Most of the code, tests and documentation were generated with an AI coding agent from our instructions, then reviewed and tested by the team. No AI model runs in the application, no data value comes from an AI model, and no AI-generated images are used. The full disclosure is in the repository README.
